words.origin: From the past participle of *variegate*. First known use: 1615.
examples: The **variegated** ivy had grown over the door by the time they came back from the war.

words.definition: To foretell the future; to make prophecies
words.origin: From Latin *vaticinatus*, past participle of *vaticinari* "to prophesy", from *vates* "seer, prophet". First known use: circa 1623.
examples: The Delphic priestess would **vaticinate** in hexameters, for a goat.

words.definition: The forefront or vanguard
words.origin: From Middle English *vauntwarde*, from Anglo-French *avantwarde* "vanguard". A doublet of *vanguard* and *avant-garde*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: In the **vaward** of the charge rode the Duke, by mistake.

words.definition: Forceful, passionate, and intense; also, angry and violent
words.origin: From Middle French, from Latin *vehemens* "violent, forceful", of uncertain derivation. First known use: 15th century.
examples: His **vehement** denials could be heard at the far end of the Rideau Canal.

words.definition: The faintest wish or inclination, too weak to lead to action
words.origin: From Medieval Latin *velleitas*, from Latin *velle* "to wish, will". First known use: 1618.
examples: He had a **velleity** to write, which lasted out his life in Paris.

words.definition: Fine parchment made from calf, lamb, or kid skin, used for writing or binding; also, high-quality cream paper
words.origin: From Middle English *velym*, from Anglo-French *velin* "of a calf", from *veel* "calf". First known use: 14th century.
examples: On **vellum** the Treaty was signed, by men who could read it and men who could not.

words.definition: Soft and velvety, covered with fine, dense hairs, as some leaves
words.origin: From New Latin *velutinus* "velvety", + *-ous*. Compare Italian *velluto* "velvet".
examples: **Velutinous** moss had grown over the Roman's name in the wall.

words.definition: Open to bribery; corrupt; also, able to be bought
words.origin: From Latin *venalis* "purchasable, on sale", formed from *venum* "sale". First known use: 1652.
examples: A **venal** customs officer in Halifax waved through the Tsar's emeralds.

words.definition: Commanding respect because of age, wisdom, or character; as a noun, a title for an archdeacon or a person declared holy
words.origin: From Latin *venerabilis* "worthy of respect", from *venerari* "to revere", partly by way of Anglo-French. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The **venerable** Bede lies in Durham, as patient as the rain.

words.definition: To regard with deep respect or reverence
words.origin: From Latin *veneratus*, past participle of *venerari* "to worship, revere". First known use: circa 1623.
examples: In Quebec they **venerate** a saint's forearm, kept behind glass.

words.definition: Hunting; the chase; also, the pursuit of sexual pleasure
words.origin: From Middle English *venerie* "hunting", from Old French, from *vener* "to hunt", from Latin *venari*. In the sense of sexual pursuit, from Latin *venus* "sexual desire". First known use: 14th century.
examples: In the arts of **venery**, the Queen's huntsman had no equal and two families.

words.definition: Having a big belly; also, gluttonous
words.origin: From Middle French *ventripotent*, formed from Latin *venter* "belly" and *potens* "mighty".
examples: The **ventripotent** monk blocked the abbey door and could not be got round.

words.definition: Truthfulness; habitual honesty; also, accuracy or conformity to the facts
words.origin: From Medieval Latin *veracitas* "truthfulness", from Latin *verax* "truthful", from *verus* "true". First known use: 1614.
examples: Her **veracity** was never in doubt; that was the trouble with having her to dinner.

words.definition: Excessive, wordy language with little meaning; also, the way something is worded
words.origin: From French *verbiage*, from Middle French *verbier* "to warble, gabble", its spelling influenced by *verbe* "word". First known use: circa 1721.
examples: Under all the **verbiage**, the treaty gave away Alsace.

words.definition: To repeat meaningless words or phrases over and over, especially as a symptom of mental illness
words.origin: From Latin *verbigerare* "to chat", from *verbum* "word" + *gerere* "to carry on".
examples: In the east wing, he would **verbigerate** the names of the Kings of Israel till dawn.

words.definition: An obsession with words; also, abnormal talkativeness
words.origin: From Latin *verbum* "word" + *mania*.
examples: Her **verbomania** ran through three dictionaries and the patience of the librarian.

words.definition: Using more words than needed; wordy and long-winded
words.origin: From Latin *verbosus* "wordy", from *verbum* "word". First known use: circa 1531.
examples: A **verbose** Member rose at midnight to discuss the herring.

words.definition: Lush and green with growing plants; also, inexperienced or naive
words.origin: From Middle French *verdoyant* "becoming green", present participle of *verdoyer*, from *vert* "green", from Latin *viridis*. First known use: 1581.
examples: A **verdant** youth came to the city, with a good coat and his mother's advice.

words.definition: Of a blue-green, sea-coloured hue
words.origin: From Italian *verdazzurro* "sea-green", from *verde* "green" + *azzurro* "blue".
examples: The **verdazurine** water of the cove closed over the anchor and kept its secret.

words.definition: The green or bluish coating that forms on copper, brass, or bronze exposed to air
words.origin: From Middle English *vertegrese*, from Anglo-French *vert de Grece* "green of Greece". First known use: 14th century.
examples: **Verdigris** had crept up the Admiral's bronze legs as far as the sword.

words.definition: Bashful; modest
words.origin: From Latin *verecundus* "shy, modest", from *vereri* "to feel awe, fear".
examples: The **verecund** young clerk blushed at the mention of a table's legs.

words.definition: Having the appearance of truth; probable; also, realistic
words.origin: From Latin *verisimilis* "probable, truth-like", from *veri*, genitive of *verum* "truth", + *similis* "like", with the suffix *-ar*. First known use: 1681.
examples: Her **verisimilar** account of the fire took in everything except her part in it.

words.definition: The appearance of being true or real; lifelikeness
words.origin: From Latin *verisimilitudo* "likeness to truth", from *veri* "of the truth" + *similitudo* "likeness". First known use: circa 1576.
examples: For **verisimilitude**, the painter added one dead fly to the Duchess's fruit.

words.definition: So moved by emotion as to be unable to speak; also, flustered
words.origin: From Yiddish *farklemt* "choked up, distraught", past participle of a verb meaning "to press, pinch". The spelling follows German *ver-*. First known use: 1991.
examples: He stood **verklempt** at the door, holding the small shoes she had left behind.

words.definition: Marked with fine, wavy, wormlike lines; also, worm-eaten, or intricately winding
words.origin: From Latin *vermiculatus* "inlaid in wavy lines", from *vermiculus* "little worm", from *vermis* "worm". First known use: 1605.
examples: Those **vermiculate** tracks under the elm's bark spelled out its death.

words.definition: The everyday language spoken by ordinary people of a place; as an adjective, native or local, as in a local style of building
words.origin: From Latin *vernaculus* "native, of the home", from *verna*, a slave born in the master's household. First known use: 1601.
examples: In the **vernacular** of the Glasgow shipyards, the Minister was then described.

words.definition: Relating to spring; also, fresh and youthful
words.origin: From Latin *vernalis*, formed from *vernus* "springtime", from *ver* "spring". First known use: 1530.
examples: A **vernal** wind came through the sickroom and lifted all the prescriptions.

words.definition: The left-hand page of a book, or the back of a sheet of paper
words.origin: From Latin *verso folio* "on the turned leaf", from *vertere* "to turn". First known use: 1839.
examples: On the **verso** of the deed, in pencil, she had written the name of the real father.

words.definition: In sociology, understanding human behaviour through empathy, from the actor's own point of view
words.origin: From German *Verstehen* "understanding", from *verstehen* "to understand".
examples: Her book on the bank tellers rested on **verstehen**, and on three years in a cage.

words.definition: Causing dizziness, as from a great height; also, whirling, or fickle and changeable
words.origin: From Latin *vertiginosus* "dizzy", from *vertigo* "a whirling, giddiness", partly by way of Middle French. First known use: 1608.
examples: From the **vertiginous** top of the bell tower, the town looked as if it could be forgiven.

words.definition: Relating to or happening in the evening; also, of flowers or animals, opening or active at dusk
words.origin: From Latin *vespertinus* "of the evening", from *vesper* "evening". First known use: 15th century.
examples: The **vespertine** primroses opened at dusk, for no one, along the wall of the asylum.

words.definition: Remaining as a small trace of something that once existed; of a body part, shrunken and no longer useful
words.origin: From Latin *vestigium*, the source of *vestige*, + *-al*. First known use: 1843.
examples: A **vestigial** politeness made the hangman ask if the rope was too tight.

words.definition: Annoying and troublesome; in law, of a lawsuit, brought without good grounds just to harass
words.origin: From *vexation* + *-ous*.
examples: Her **vexatious** lawsuits against the Hudson's Bay Company ran for forty years.

words.definition: Holy Communion given to a dying person; also, provisions or money for a journey
words.origin: From Latin *viaticum* "travelling money, supplies for a journey", a noun use of *viaticus*, from *via* "road". First known use: 1562.
examples: He took the **viaticum** in a trench at Passchendaele, from a chaplain with no legs.

words.definition: Experienced through imagining another's experience; also, done or suffered in place of another
words.origin: From Latin *vicarius* "substituting, deputy", from *vicis* "change, turn, stead", + *-ous*. A doublet of *vicar*. First known use: 1637.
examples: Reading Byron by the stove, the spinster enjoyed a **vicarious** Greece.

words.definition: A neighbourhood or surrounding district; also, its residents, or nearness
words.origin: From Middle English *vesinage*, from Anglo-French *veisinage*, from *veisin* "neighbouring", from Latin *vicinus* "near"; later respelled after the Latin. First known use: 14th century.
examples: The whole **vicinage** turned out to watch her leave him, and brought folding chairs.

words.definition: A change of circumstances or fortune, usually unwelcome; also, changeableness
words.origin: From Latin *vicissitudo* "alteration", formed on *vicissim* "by turns", which comes from *vicis* "change", partly by way of Middle French. First known use: circa 1576.
examples: Each **vicissitude** of the wheat price could be read in her mother's hats.

words.definition: Food supplies; provisions, usually in the plural; as a verb, to supply with food
words.origin: From Middle English *vitaille*, from Anglo-French, from Late Latin *victualia* "provisions", from Latin *victus* "nourishment", from *vivere* "to live". First known use: 15th century.
examples: To **victual** the fort, they ate the horses, then the harness.

words.definition: Based on the number twenty; counting in twenties
words.origin: From Latin *vigesimus* "twentieth", a variant of *vicesimus*, influenced by *viginti* "twenty", + *-al*. First known use: circa 1656.
examples: Old market women in Wales still sold by a **vigesimal** reckoning of their own.

words.definition: To speak or write about someone in an abusive, defamatory way; to disparage
words.origin: From Late Latin *vilificare*, from Latin *vilis* "cheap, worthless". First known use: 15th century.
examples: The papers would **vilify** him until the day he died and then put up a statue.

words.definition: Having the colour of red wine; also, relating to wine or grapes
words.origin: From Latin *vinaceus*, an adjective formed from *vinum* "wine". First known use: 1678.
examples: The **vinaceous** stain on the tablecloth was the sole survivor of that dinner.

words.definition: To clear someone of blame or suspicion; also, to prove right or justified
words.origin: From Latin *vindicatus*, past participle of *vindicare* "to lay claim to; to set free; to avenge", from *vindex* "claimant, avenger". First known use: circa 1571.
examples: One small letter in a shoebox would **vindicate** her, forty years too late to matter.

words.definition: A loud, domineering, bad-tempered woman; formerly, a woman of great strength and courage
words.origin: From Latin *virago* "heroic woman", from *vir* "man", with a suffix expressing resemblance. First known use: 14th century.
examples: That **virago** of the Klondike ran off two claim jumpers with a soup ladle.

words.definition: Turning green; greenish
words.origin: From Latin *virescens* "turning green", from *virescere*, an inceptive form of *virere* "to be green". First known use: 1826.
examples: A **virescent** tinge crept over the Dauphin's face on the crossing to Dover.

words.definition: Streaks of rain or snow hanging below a cloud that vanish in the air before touching land
words.origin: From Latin *virga* "rod, branch; a streak in the sky". First known use: 1938.
examples: **Virga** hung from the cloud above the dying wheat, never reaching it.

words.definition: Bright green; verdant
words.origin: From Latin *viridis* "green", from *virere* "to be green". First known use: 1600.
examples: The **virid** moss had got into the sundial and stopped it at a quarter past Waterloo.

words.definition: Greenness, as of fresh grass and leaves; also, youthful innocence
words.origin: From Latin *viriditas* "greenness", from *viridis* "green", partly by way of Old French. First known use: 15th century.
examples: The **viridity** of the Irish hills made the exiled bishop put down his glass.

words.definition: A love of or taste for fine art objects and curios; also, such objects collectively
words.origin: From Italian *virtù* "excellence, virtue", from Latin *virtus*. First known use: 1722.
examples: His cabinet of **virtu** held a Roman coin, a saint's knuckle, and his first wife's teeth.

words.definition: Showing dazzling technical skill, especially in music
words.origin: From *virtuoso* + *-ic*. First known use: 1879.
examples: Her **virtuosic** lying was the only art that was ever practised in that town.

words.definition: Of a disease or poison, severe, fast-spreading, or deadly; also, bitterly hostile
words.origin: From Latin *virulentus* "poisonous", from *virus* "venom, poison". In Middle English it was used of wounds discharging pus. First known use: 14th century.
examples: A **virulent** review of her poems reached Winnipeg before the poet did.

words.definition: A person's face or expression; also, the appearance of something
words.origin: From Anglo-French *visage*, from *vis* "face", from Latin *visus* "sight, appearance", from *videre* "to see". First known use: 14th century.
examples: His **visage** was on the stamps; his creditors licked it with some satisfaction.

words.definition: Thick and sticky; glutinous
words.origin: From Late Latin *viscidus* "sticky", from Latin *viscum* "mistletoe; birdlime made from its berries". First known use: 1635.
examples: A **viscid** honey moved down the bread as slowly as the Sunday sermon.

words.definition: Thick and sticky, flowing slowly
words.origin: From Late Latin *viscosus* "full of birdlime", from Latin *viscum* "mistletoe, birdlime", partly by way of Anglo-French. First known use: 14th century.
examples: Down the street came a **viscous** tide of molasses at thirty-five miles an hour.

words.definition: To spoil, weaken, or make faulty; also, to make legally invalid, or to corrupt morally
words.origin: From Latin *vitiatus*, past participle of *vitiare* "to spoil, impair", from *vitium* "fault, defect". First known use: 1534.
examples: One small lie would **vitiate** the whole contract, and also, in time, the marriage.

words.definition: Bitterly harsh, caustic criticism; also, sulphuric acid or its metallic salts
words.origin: From Old French *vitriol*, from Medieval Latin *vitriolum*, from Latin *vitrum* "glass".
examples: Her letters to the Globe were pure **vitriol**, and beautifully spelled.

words.definition: To berate or attack with harsh, abusive language
words.origin: From Latin *vituperatus*, past participle of *vituperare* "to blame, find fault with", from *vitium* "fault" + *parare* "to prepare". First known use: 1542.
examples: From a soapbox at Speakers' Corner he would **vituperate** the moon.

words.definition: Lively, animated, and full of high spirits
words.origin: From Latin *vivax* "long-lived, lively", from *vivere* "to live", + *-ous*. First known use: circa 1645.
examples: A **vivacious** corpse sat up at the wake and asked for a drink.

words.definition: Strikingly bright or intense; also, producing clear, lifelike images in the mind
words.origin: From Latin *vividus* "lively, animated", from *vivere* "to live". First known use: 1634.
examples: His most **vivid** memory of the war was of a small, very clean horse.

words.definition: Loudly and insistently outspoken; clamorous
words.origin: From Latin *vociferari* "to shout, cry out" + *-ous*. First known use: 1700.
examples: A **vociferous** minority of geese held the Parliament lawn.

words.definition: The power of choosing or deciding by one's own will; also, a choice or decision
words.origin: From French *volition*, from Medieval Latin *volitio* "will", from Latin *velle* "to wish, will". First known use: 1605.
examples: Of his own **volition**, the cat walked into the river, and the village still talks of it.

words.definition: A turn, in music or poetry, especially the shift in thought in a sonnet; also, a lively Renaissance dance
words.origin: From Italian *volta* "a turn; a time".
examples: At the sonnet's **volta**, she stopped being in love, and went on for six more lines.

words.definition: A complete reversal of opinion or policy; an about-face
words.origin: From French *volte-face*, from Italian *voltafaccia*, made up of *voltare* "to turn" and *faccia* "face". First known use: 1819.
examples: The Minister's **volte-face** on the railway came shortly after dinner with the railway.

words.definition: Talking fluently, readily, and at length
words.origin: From Latin *volubilis* "turning easily, flowing", from *volvere* "to roll, turn". In Middle English it meant "changeable". First known use: 15th century.
examples: The **voluble** parrot gave its evidence in the voice of the second Mrs. Ames.

words.definition: Having a huge appetite; also, extremely eager, as a reader who devours books
words.origin: From Latin *vorax* "devouring, greedy", from *vorare* "to devour", + *-ious*. First known use: 1599.
examples: A **voracious** reader, the boy got through the Bible, the almanac, and the wallpaper.

words.definition: An abyss, chasm, or gulf
words.origin: From Latin *vorago* "abyss".
examples: The bank's collapse opened a **vorago** under the whole of Main Street.

words.definition: Sharp or deadly, as a blade
words.origin: Coined by Lewis Carroll in the poem "Jabberwocky", perhaps modelled on *warp* and *vortex*.
examples: Up came his **vorpal** butter knife; the toast never stood a chance.

words.definition: A devoted follower or admirer of a cause or pursuit; also, someone bound by religious vows, such as a monk or nun
words.origin: From Latin *votum* "vow", from *vovere* "to vow", + *-ary*. First known use: 1543.
examples: A lifelong **votary** of the racetrack, he wanted his ashes scattered on the far turn.

words.definition: A remedy used to heal wounds; as an adjective, useful in healing wounds
words.origin: From Latin *vulnerarius* "of wounds", from *vulnus* "wound". First known use: 1599.
examples: Her grandmother's **vulnerary** of comfrey and lard had closed up three generations of boys.

words.definition: Like a fox; also, cunning and crafty
words.origin: From Latin *vulpinus* "fox-like", from *vulpes* "fox". First known use: 15th century.
examples: A **vulpine** grin crossed the auctioneer's face as the widow raised her hand.

words.definition: Exhausted and worn out; Scottish
words.origin: From Scots *wabbit*, of uncertain origin; perhaps from earlier *wobart* "withered, feeble".
examples: She came home **wabbit** from the mill and started in on the washing.

words.definition: In Japanese aesthetics, a quiet, simple, or solitary beauty found in plain and rustic things
words.origin: From Japanese *wabi*.
examples: One cracked cup on a bare shelf: that was all the **wabi** she could afford.

words.definition: A Japanese way of finding beauty in imperfection, simplicity, and the passing of time
words.origin: From Japanese, combining *wabi* "austere beauty" with *sabi* "aged appearance". First known use: 1963.
examples: Her son called the leaning shed **wabi-sabi**, and she told him to fix the roof.

words.definition: Playfully humorous and mischievous
words.origin: From *wag* "rogue" + *-ish*. First known use: 1589.
examples: A **waggish** telegraphist added "Love" to the Prime Minister's cable.

words.definition: Wooden panelling lining the lower part of an interior wall; as a verb, to line with such panelling
words.origin: From Middle Dutch or Middle Low German *wagenschot*, probably from *wagen* "wagon" + *schot* "partition, crossbar". First known use: 14th century.
examples: Behind the **wainscot**, something small kept on counting the family's money.

words.definition: To move unsteadily or with a rolling, weaving motion; also, of the stomach, to churn or rumble with nausea
words.origin: From Middle English *wamlen*, of obscure origin; compare Danish *vamle* "to feel sick" and Norwegian *vamla* "to stagger". First known use: 14th century.
examples: His stomach would **wamble** at the first sound of her good china being laid.

words.definition: A strong urge to travel and wander
words.origin: From German *Wanderlust*, from *wandern* "to wander, hike" + *Lust* "desire, pleasure". First known use: 1875.
examples: His **wanderlust** came on each spring, and each spring she checked his boots.

words.definition: To decrease gradually in size, strength, or intensity; of the moon, to show less of its lit face
words.origin: From Old English *wanian* "to lessen", related to *wan-* "lacking". First known use: before 12th century.
examples: As his fortunes began to **wane**, his friends began to discover the country.

words.definition: Despair; hopelessness; also, a vain or delusive hope
words.origin: From Middle English *wanhope*, from *wan-* "lacking" + *hope*. Compare Dutch *wanhoop* "despair".
examples: In his **wanhope**, the lighthouse keeper stopped winding the lamp.

words.definition: Unrestrained and undisciplined; also, deliberately cruel or reckless, or lewd, or playful
words.origin: From Middle English *wantowen* "undisciplined, ill-bred", from *wan-* "not" + *towen* "brought up, trained", from Old English *teon* "to draw, rear". First known use: 14th century.
examples: With **wanton** cruelty, the small boy pulled the wings from each of her fine excuses.

words.definition: A fool; someone lacking sense
words.origin: From *want* + *wit*.
examples: The **wantwit** at the gate was the only one who'd seen who came and went.

words.definition: Cautious and watchful, alert to danger or deception
words.origin: From the adjective *ware* "watchful, cautious" + *-y*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: A **wary** moose looked up from the CPR's newest siding.

words.definition: A good-for-nothing who squanders time or money; also, a neglected child, or refuse
words.origin: From *waste* + the disparaging suffix *-rel*. First known use: circa 1841.
examples: The family **wastrel** came home with a cough and a very good story.

words.definition: An annual outing or feast held for the workers of a printing house
words.origin: Of unknown origin; the earlier form was *waygoose*.
examples: At the **wayzgoose**, three compositors fell into the Thames, justified.

words.definition: The sky; the vault of heaven; also, the upper air
words.origin: From Old English *wolcen* "cloud", whose plural meant "the heavens". First known use: 12th century.
examples: Their hymn rang the **welkin** as the ship began to go down by the stern.

words.definition: A comprehensive view or philosophy of the world and humanity's place in it
words.origin: From German *Weltanschauung*, from *Welt* "world" + *Anschauung* "view, perception". First known use: 1868.
examples: His entire **weltanschauung** rested on the belief that the Liberals had stolen his bicycle.

words.definition: A confused mass or jumble; as a verb, to wallow, or to toss about, as waves
words.origin: From Middle English *welteren* "to tumble, writhe", a frequentative of *welten* "to overturn", from Old English *weltan* "to roll". First known use: 14th century.
examples: In a **welter** of feathers, the pillow fight ended the Peace Conference.

words.definition: A weary sadness at the state of the world compared with how it ought to be; world-weariness
words.origin: From German *Weltschmerz* "world-pain", from *Welt* "world" + *Schmerz* "pain". First known use: 1864.
examples: He suffered from **weltschmerz**, his mother said, and also from not having a job.

words.definition: A harmless cyst or lump on the skin, especially the scalp; also, a large, overcrowded city
words.origin: From Old English *wenn*, related to Dutch *wen*. First known use: before 12th century.
examples: The great **wen** of London swallowed the boy, and sent back a very occasional postcard.

words.definition: The essential nature of a thing; what makes it what it is
words.origin: From *what* + *-ness*.
examples: Aquinas pondered the **whatness** of the angel, and left the soup to cool.

words.definition: To coax or persuade by flattery or sweet talk; also, to obtain this way
words.origin: Of uncertain origin; perhaps from Middle English *wedlen* "to beg", from Old English *wædlian* "to be poor". First known use: circa 1661.
examples: She could **wheedle** a dance out of a Presbyterian.

words.definition: To engulf, bury, or submerge; also, to overwhelm
words.origin: From Middle English *whelmen* "to turn over, capsize", perhaps a blend of dialect *whelve* "to bend over" and *helm* "to cover". First known use: 14th century.
examples: Slowly the tide would **whelm** the causeway as the monks ran for it.

words.definition: Of a horse, to neigh softly; also, to snicker; as a noun, a soft neigh
words.origin: Of imitative origin. Compare German *wiehern* "to neigh". First known use: 1753.
examples: Her mare would **whicker** at the gate, a whole winter after she died.

words.definition: Of the wind, to blow in light, shifting gusts; also, to waver or vacillate, or to make a soft whistling sound
words.origin: Probably a frequentative of *whiff*, formed with *-le*. First known use: 1568.
examples: Round the tent pegs the wind would **whiffle**, then drop, then think again.

words.definition: Former; one-time; as an adverb, formerly
words.origin: From Old English *hwilum* "at times", a dative plural form of *hwil* "a while, a time". First known use: 12th century.
examples: Her **whilom** husband waved from the other side of the customs shed.

words.definition: Playfully quaint or fanciful; also, unpredictable and capricious
words.origin: From *whimsy* + *-ical*. First known use: 1653.
examples: The **whimsical** old Earl left his fortune to whichever nephew could make him laugh.

words.definition: Playful, fanciful humour; also, an odd or fanciful idea, or a passing fancy
words.origin: Probably from *whim* or *whim-wham* + *-sy*. First known use: 1605.
examples: In a moment of **whimsy**, she married him.

words.definition: To grumble and complain fretfully and persistently; mainly British
words.origin: From a northern form of Old English *hwinsian* "to whine", related to Old High German *winson* "to moan". First known use: 12th century.
examples: He would **whinge** about the tea all the way up Everest.

words.definition: A young, cheeky, presumptuous person
words.origin: Probably an altered form of *snippersnapper*, perhaps blended with *whipster*. First known use: 1700.
examples: That **whippersnapper** from Cambridge told Rutherford he had dropped something.

words.definition: A child's spinning toy, such as a top or pinwheel; also, anything that whirls or keeps changing, or a giddy person
words.origin: From Middle English *whirlegigg*, a compound of *whirlen* "to whirl" and *gigg* "top". First known use: 15th century.
examples: The **whirligig** on the barn roof kept on turning for a farm that had long since stopped.

words.definition: Hush; be quiet; mainly Irish and Scottish
words.origin: From Middle English *whist*, of imitative origin. First known use: 14th century.
examples: "**Whisht**," said his granny, listening hard at the keyhole.

words.definition: Anticlockwise; in the wrong or contrary direction
words.origin: From Middle Low German *weddersinnes*, from *wedder-* "against" + *sin* "direction, way". First known use: 1545.
examples: Three times **widdershins** she went around the kirk, and the minister's cow fell ill.

words.definition: Any of several freshwater ducks related to the mallard; formerly, a fool
words.origin: Of uncertain origin; perhaps from an Anglo-French form related to French *vigeon*. First known use: 1508.
examples: A lone **widgeon** came down on the flooded cricket pitch, at silly mid-off.

words.definition: Silly, scatterbrained, or ditzy; also, vague and insubstantial
words.origin: Of unknown origin. First known use: 1918.
examples: The **wifty** young heiress gave her diamonds to a very surprised bus driver.

words.definition: A living creature, especially a human being; also, a ghost or supernatural being; formerly, as an adjective, valiant
words.origin: From Old English *wiht* "creature, thing", related to German *Wicht*. First known use: before 12th century.
examples: The poor **wight** in the ditch turned out to be the Member for Kings County.

words.definition: Whether one likes it or not; also, haphazardly, without order or plan
words.origin: From the phrase *will I, nill I* "whether I wish or not", or *will ye, nill ye*. First known use: 1608.
examples: **Willy-nilly**, the Mennonite boy went off to the war in a cattle car.

words.definition: Someone who secretly manipulates people or events from behind the scenes
words.origin: From *wire* + *puller*, suggesting one who works a puppet.
examples: In a Montreal back room, the **wirepuller** chewed his cigar and named a premier.

words.definition: A know-it-all who pretends to wisdom or cleverness; a smart aleck
words.origin: From Middle Dutch *wijssegger* "soothsayer", altered from Old High German *wizzago* "prophet" as though made of words for *wise* and *say*. First known use: 1595.
examples: The village **wiseacre** told the drowning man that he should have learned to swim.

words.definition: Knew; past tense of an old verb meaning to know
words.origin: The past tense of *wit* "to know", from Old English *witan*; also treated as an altered form of *wis*. First known use: 1508.
examples: Little she **wist** what the morning would bring, as she set the good bread to rise.

words.definition: Full of yearning tinged with melancholy; sadly thoughtful
words.origin: Probably from obsolete *wist* "quiet, attentive", a variant of *whist*, + *-ful*, influenced by obsolete *wistly* "intently". First known use: 1714.
examples: A **wistful** bear in a Moscow circus looked north all through the waltz.

words.definition: An Anglo-Saxon council of nobles and churchmen that advised the king; also, a session of it
words.origin: From Old English *witena gemot* "assembly of the wise", from *wita* "councillor, sage" + *gemot* "meeting". First known use: before 12th century.
examples: The **witenagemot** met in the rain and agreed that the king was, on balance, unwell.

words.definition: A husband who knowingly puts up with his wife's unfaithfulness; also, a witless person
words.origin: From Middle English *wetewold*, from *weten* "to know" + *cokewold* "cuckold". First known use: 15th century.
examples: That cheerful **wittol** held her coat for the Marquess, tipping him on the way out.

words.definition: To shrivel, wither, and wrinkle, as with age; as an adjective, shrivelled
words.origin: From Old English *wisnian* "to wither", related to Old Norse *visna*.
examples: Apples would **wizen** in the attic through the long Ontario winter.

words.definition: Looking sad, sorrowful, and miserable; also, in a sorry state
words.origin: From Middle English *wo begon* "beset by woe", from *wo* + *begon*, past participle of *begon* "to go about, beset". First known use: 14th century.
examples: A **woebegone** scarecrow stood guard over the last field the bank hadn't taken.

words.definition: An area of high, open, rolling country, used in English place names
words.origin: From Old English *wald* "forest", related to German *Wald*. First known use: before 12th century.
examples: Sheep grazed the Yorkshire **wold** where the Danes had come ashore and burned it.

words.definition: To be given to doing something habitually; as an adjective, accustomed; as a noun, a habit or usual practice
words.origin: From Old English *gewunod* "accustomed", the past participle of *gewunian* "to dwell, be used to". First known use: before 12th century.
examples: The Chief Justice was **wont** to wake and sentence the wrong man.

words.definition: Idle daydreaming; absent-mindedness
words.origin: From *wool* + *gathering*.
examples: The young clerk was **woolgathering** when the bank was robbed, and wrote a poem about it.

words.definition: A hobgoblin or bogey; also, anything frightful or grotesque, or a scary-looking person
words.origin: From *worry* "to harass" + *cow*.
examples: The tax man at the door was a proper **worricow**, to Great-Uncle Fergus's mind.

words.definition: Ruinous; destructive
words.origin: From *wrack* "ruin, destruction" + *-ful*. First known use: 1558.
examples: The **wrackful** siege of winter had left them with a single goat and a good many hymns.

words.definition: A ghost, especially the image of a living person seen just before or after their death; also, anything pale and insubstantial
words.origin: Of uncertain origin; originally Scots. It may be related to Scots *wraith* "anger", or to Old Norse *vörthr* "guardian". First known use: 1513.
examples: A pale **wraith** of a girl came up from the shore, and asked if her father was home.

words.definition: Twisted, coiled, or contorted
words.origin: From Old English *writhen*, past participle of *writhan* "to twist". First known use: before 12th century.
examples: Those **writhen** olive trees had seen Pilate go by, and said nothing.

words.definition: Unjust, unlawful, or improper
words.origin: From Middle English *wrongous*, earlier *wrongwis*, from Old English *wrangwis*, equivalent to *wrong* + *-wise*, later treated as *-ous*.
examples: He'd been imprisoned for **wrongous** cause, he said, and also for the sheep.

words.definition: Dryly, often ironically humorous; also, twisted or contorted, as a wry face
words.origin: From an obsolete verb *wry* "to twist", from Old English *wrigian* "to turn, swerve, strive". First known use: 14th century.
examples: She gave a **wry** smile as they lowered the second husband in beside the first.

words.definition: A child prodigy; also, someone who achieves remarkable success at a young age
words.origin: From German *Wunderkind*, literally "wonder child". First known use: 1873.
examples: The town's **wunderkind** had gone to Paris and come back selling very good insurance.

words.definition: Yellowish in colour
words.origin: From French *xanthique*, from *xantho-* "yellow" + *-ique*.
examples: A **xanthic** glow came over the Lachine Canal from the new soap works.

words.definition: Relating to hospitality between host and guest; friendly and welcoming
words.origin: From Greek *xenia* "hospitality" + *-al*.
examples: In a **xenial** gesture, the Bedouin killed his last goat for the lost Englishman.

words.definition: Someone attracted to foreign people, cultures, or customs
words.origin: From *xeno-* "foreign" + *-phile* "lover", perhaps after French *xénophile*. First known use: 1948.
examples: A **xenophile** in Moose Factory ordered her hats from Constantinople.

words.definition: Very dry; also, adapted to a very dry habitat
words.origin: From Greek *xeros* "dry" + *-ic*. First known use: 1926.
examples: In the **xeric** hills above Kamloops, the sagebrush has its own opinion of rain.

words.definition: Living in or growing on wood, like certain fungi and wood-boring beetles
words.origin: From *xylo-* "wood" + *-philous* "loving".
examples: **Xylophilous** beetles had got into Nelson's flagship; the Navy took it personally.

words.definition: To talk loudly, persistently, and often annoyingly; also, to complain or whine
words.origin: From Middle English *yameren*, partly from Middle Dutch *jammeren*, replacing *yomeren* "to lament", from Old English *geomrian* "to complain". First known use: 15th century.
examples: The gulls would **yammer** above the fish plant until the whistle shut them up.

words.definition: To call or name
words.origin: From Old English *cleopian* "to call, cry out, summon".
examples: They **clepe** him Noah in the village, for reasons to do with the basement.

words.definition: A person born in the same year as oneself; a contemporary
words.origin: Of uncertain origin.
examples: He met his **yealing** on the far bench, and neither of them could remember the war.

words.definition: A young lamb or kid; as an adjective, newborn
words.origin: From *yean*, a verb used of sheep and goats giving birth, + *-ling*.
examples: The small **yeanling** stood up in the sleet and looked around at what it had been given.

words.definition: To long persistently or wistfully for something; formerly, to feel tender compassion
words.origin: From Old English *giernan* "to desire", from *georn* "eager", related to German *gern* "gladly". First known use: before 12th century.
examples: She would **yearn** all her life for a man who had once held a door for her in Halifax.

words.definition: A farmer who owns and works a small estate; also, a loyal, dependable worker, or an attendant in a royal household
words.origin: From Middle English *yeman*, *yoman*, of disputed origin; perhaps a reduced form of *yongman* "young man". First known use: 14th century.
examples: A **yeoman** of Kent stood up in the court and refused the King's shilling.

words.definition: The evening of the day before
words.origin: From Old English *giestranæfen*, a compound meaning "the evening of yesterday", that is, *yester-* and *eve*.
examples: Only **yestereve**, she'd been dancing on that floor, and now they'd brought the sheets.

words.definition: Last night
words.origin: From Old English *gystran niht*, formed from *giestran* "of yesterday" and *niht* "night". First known use: before 12th century.
examples: **Yesternight** the wind brought down the Laird's chimney on the Laird.

words.definition: Yesterday evening; last night; Scottish
words.origin: From Middle English (Scots) *yistrevin*, from *yister-* (as in *yesterday*) + *evin* "evening". First known use: 1773.
examples: **Yestreen** she'd seen the new moon with the old one in its arms.

words.definition: Prestige, pedigree, or social status
words.origin: From Yiddish *yikhus*.
examples: For all his **yichus**, he could not get a table at Schwartz's.

words.definition: A naive, unsophisticated country person; a bumpkin
words.origin: Of uncertain origin; perhaps from dialect *yokel* "green woodpecker", or from dialect German *Jokel*, a diminutive of *Jakob*. First known use: circa 1819.
examples: The **yokel** in the straw hat had bought the Brooklyn Bridge, and sold it back at a profit.

words.definition: Anxious; also, absent-minded or vacant
examples: She had gone **yonderly** since the war, setting a place for the boy.

words.definition: The distant past; olden times
words.origin: From Old English *geara* "long ago", probably related to *gear* "year". First known use: 14th century.
examples: In days of **yore**, the Bishop of Bath hanged people for less than that.

words.definition: Having a full, rounded, pleasingly plump figure
words.origin: From Yiddish *zaftik* "juicy", from *zaft* "juice, sap". Compare German *saftig*. First known use: 1926.
examples: That **zaftig** Rubens nude had hung for decades over the Temperance Hall piano.

words.definition: A holder, often ornamental metal, for a handleless hot coffee cup; also, a cardboard sleeve for a hot drink
words.origin: Probably from Ottoman Turkish *zarf*, which goes back to Arabic *zarf* "vessel, sheath".
examples: The little silver **zarf** was all that remained of the Sultan's coffee and the Sultan.

words.definition: A fanatical, uncompromising supporter of a cause; originally, a member of a Jewish sect that resisted Roman rule
words.origin: From Late Latin *zelotes*, from Greek *zelotes* "emulator, zealous follower", from *zelos* "zeal". In Middle English it was an epithet of the apostle Simon. First known use: 1537.
examples: A **zealot** on Masada looked down at the Roman ramp and sharpened something.

words.definition: Full of fervent enthusiasm and devotion
words.origin: From Medieval Latin *zelosus*, from *zelus* "zeal", from Greek *zelos*. A doublet of *jealous*. First known use: 15th century.
examples: A **zealous** young customs man searched the Pope.

words.definition: The spirit of the times; the general outlook and mood of an era
words.origin: From German *Zeitgeist* "spirit of the age", from *Zeit* "time" + *Geist* "spirit". First known use: 1835.
examples: He caught the **zeitgeist** in one small song, then spent thirty years in Florida.

words.definition: The highest point or peak of something; in astronomy, the point in the sky directly overhead
words.origin: From Middle English *cenyth*, from Old French and Medieval Latin, from Arabic *samt ar-ra's* "path over the head". The *n* arose from a scribal misreading of *m*. First known use: 14th century.
examples: At the **zenith** of her fame, she could not get her own mother to come to the theatre.

words.definition: A number multiplied by itself; its square
words.origin: From New Latin *zenzicus*, from a German form of Latin *census*, by way of Italian *censo*, which medieval mathematicians used for a squared number.
examples: Diophantus would write a **zenzic** on the wet sand, and the tide marked it.

words.definition: A number raised to the eighth power
words.origin: Coined by Robert Recorde in his mathematics book *The Whetstone of Witte*, from *zenzic* "square".
examples: The monk's **zenzizenzizenzic** came out to a very large number and a very long night.

words.definition: A soft, gentle breeze; originally, the west wind; also, a fine, light fabric
words.origin: From Latin *zephyrus* "west wind", from Greek *Zephyros*, the god of the west wind. First known use: 1567.
examples: A small **zephyr** came in at the window and turned the page of the dead man's Bible.

words.definition: Breezy, soft, and gentle
words.origin: From *zephyr* + *-ous*.
examples: Through her **zephyrous** muslin, the Regency could see what it wished to.

words.definition: A figure of speech in which one word governs two others in different senses, as in "she broke his car and his heart"
words.origin: From Latin *zeugma*, from Greek *zeugma* "a yoking, bond", from *zeugnynai* "to yoke, join". First known use: 15th century.
examples: "She took her hat and her leave," the novelist wrote, pleased with the **zeugma**.

words.definition: The delusion that one has turned into an animal
words.origin: From New Latin *zoanthropia*, from Greek *zoion* "animal" + *anthropos* "human being".
examples: In his **zoanthropy**, Nebuchadnezzar went out to the field and ate grass as oxen do.

words.definition: A faint, cone-shaped glow seen in the west after twilight or in the east before dawn, caused by sunlight on dust in space
words.origin: From *zodiacal* + *light*.
examples: A **zodiacal light** rose over the Saskatchewan before the sun; the dog looked at it.

words.definition: A spinning drum with slits and a strip of pictures inside that seem to move when viewed through the slits
words.origin: From Greek *zoe* "life" + *trope* "turn", an irregular formation. The name is credited to its inventor, William E. Lincoln.
examples: In the dusty **zoetrope**, a small horse went on running for a child now ninety-one.

words.definition: Restlessness in migratory animals, especially birds, at the start of the migration season
words.origin: From German *Zugunruhe*, a compound of *Zug* "migration" and *Unruhe* "restlessness, unease".
examples: In its Viennese cage, the warbler's **zugunruhe** began each September at dusk.

words.definition: In chess, a position where any move a player makes will worsen their situation; also, any such bind
words.origin: From German *Zugzwang*, literally "move compulsion", from *Zug* "move" and *Zwang* "constraint".
examples: In **zugzwang** at the Christmas table, he could praise neither sister's pudding.

words.definition: Having only one plane of symmetry, so it can be split into matching halves in only one way, as many flowers
words.origin: From *zygo-* "yoke, pair" + *-morphic* "having the form of".
examples: Mendel looked at the **zygomorphic** pea blossom, as the Abbot looked at the accounts.

words.definition: The chemistry of fermentation, as in brewing beer and making wine
words.origin: From *zym-* "fermentation" + *-urgy* "working", on the model of *metallurgy*.
examples: The friar's knowledge of **zymurgy** had filled the abbey's cellars and emptied its pews.

words.definition: Energetic style, confidence, and flair
words.origin: From French *élan*, from Middle French *eslan* "a dash, rush", from *eslancer* "to dart".
examples: She entered the bankruptcy court with considerable **élan**, and a very large hat.

words.definition: The vital life force driving evolution and creativity, in the philosophy of Henri Bergson
words.origin: From French *élan vital* "vital impetus", a term coined by the philosopher Henri Bergson.
examples: Bergson's **élan vital** got her through the seminar and the man who taught it.

words.definition: A small ornamental case for holding needles, cosmetics, or other small articles
words.origin: From French *étui*.
examples: In her ivory **étui** she carried needles, thread, and one small vial for the Count.
